topic: skirting, scouring and carding a raw Jacob fleece before spinning it over winter

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-3)
provenance.notes: napisane niezaleznie od korpusu PL, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: termometr do kapieli pluczacej

base: I have a raw Jacob fleece from a neighbour and want to spin it this winter.
A hogget fleece from the same flock lies in the other sack, much finer throughout.
I keep a bath thermometer by the sink, since hot water once felted a whole fleece.
The wool is heavy with grease and full of hay seed near the britch.
Should I skirt and pick it dry first, or wash the whole fleece straight away?
Skirt it dry first, because grease holds the dirt and washing simply spreads it about.
Lay the whole fleece out cut side down and pull away the soiled edges.
Britch wool is coarse and seedy, and no amount of washing will improve it.
Only when the fleece is clean of vegetable matter should any water touch it.
I skirted the fleece and threw out nearly a fifth of the weight.
The bath thermometer read sixty degrees when I lowered the first batch in.
The locks came out clean but they feel slightly harsh and squeaky now.
Did I strip too much grease, or is that simply how scoured wool feels?
You stripped rather too much, since sixty degrees with detergent takes out nearly all the lanolin.
Wool wants a little grease left in it to card and draft kindly.
Drop the next bath to fifty and use rather less detergent than before.
Never stir the wool while it soaks, or the fibres will lock together.
I scoured the rest at fifty degrees and the locks came out far softer.
The bath thermometer barely moved, and I left the wool completely still throughout.
That hogget fleece in the other sack has much shorter locks than this one.
Will such short wool card properly, or should I comb it instead?
Card the short wool, because combs throw away everything below about three inches long.
Carding keeps the fibres crossed and gives a light, airy yarn when spun.
Combing lays them parallel and suits only the longest, strongest staple you have.
Match the tool to the fibre and the yarn will follow of itself.
I carded the short wool into rolags and they draft beautifully off the wheel.
The longer Jacob staple I combed instead, and the top is glossy and smooth.
My rolags keep breaking up when I try to card too much at once.
How much wool belongs on a pair of hand carders at one loading?
Load far less than you think, because a thin charge cards evenly and a thick one tangles.
The teeth should just show through the wool when you look across the carder.
Three light passes give a better rolag than one heavy pass ever will.
Keep the strokes long and let the carders do the work for you.
Lighter loading fixed it and my rolags now roll off whole every time.
I have spun about half a pound and the yarn is fairly even.
The Jacob colours have blended into a soft grey I did not expect.
Should I separate the colours next time, or is the blend worth keeping?
Separate them next time, because a Jacob fleece gives you three natural colours free.
Sort the locks as you skirt, while the pattern is still plain to see.
Once they are carded together the colours can never be pulled apart again.
Keep this grey though, since blended Jacob makes a very handsome plain sweater.
